meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.stem: Suppose a housing dataset records the variables below. Which one is an indicator (dummy) variable?

options.text: Number of bedrooms, from 1 to 6
options.feedback: A count takes many values. An indicator takes only the values 0 and 1.

options.text: Region, coded 1 = North, 2 = South, 3 = West
options.feedback: This is a categorical variable with three codes. It would be represented by a set of indicators, one per region.

options.text: Pool: 1 if the house has a pool, 0 if not
options.feedback: Correct. It records membership in one category with the values 1 and 0.

options.text: Price per square foot, in dollars
options.feedback: This is a continuous variable, not a 0/1 variable.

practice.explanation: Section 14.1: an indicator variable equals 1 if an observation is in a category and 0 otherwise. Multi-category codes such as region need a set of indicators.

practice.concept: Regression on a single indicator (Section 14.1, Key Concept 14.1)
practice.stem: OLS regression of y on an intercept and an indicator d gives ŷ = 3 + 5d (Practice Exercise 1). What is the mean of y in the subsample with d = 0?

options.feedback: Correct. When d = 0, the prediction is the intercept, which equals the mean of y in that group.
5 is the coefficient on d, the difference between the two group means.
8 = 3 + 5 is the mean of y in the group with d = 1.

options.text: It cannot be found without knowing the group sizes.
options.feedback: Group sizes are not needed: with a single indicator, the intercept is exactly the d = 0 group's mean.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.1: in ŷ = b + ad, b is the mean of y when d = 0 and b + a is the mean when d = 1, so the d = 0 mean is 3 and the d = 1 mean is 8.

practice.concept: Regression on a single indicator (Section 14.1, Key Concept 14.1)
practice.stem: Suppose the mean of y is 30 in the subsample with d = 1 and 20 in the subsample with d = 0 (Practice Exercise 2). What fitted model does OLS regression of y on an intercept and d give?

options.feedback: Correct. The intercept is the d = 0 mean (20) and the slope is the difference in means, 30 − 20 = 10.
This would be the fit if d = 1 marked the group with mean 20. Here the intercept must be the d = 0 mean, 20.
25 is the average of the two means. The intercept is the mean of the d = 0 group alone.
This predicts 30 for d = 0 and 40 for d = 1; neither matches the group means.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.1: b = ȳ₀ = 20 and a = ȳ₁ − ȳ₀ = 10, so ŷ = 20 + 10d. Check: d = 1 gives 30.

practice.stem: Suppose hourly wages are regressed on an intercept, a union-membership indicator, and years of experience. Then every union member in the sample receives the same predicted wage.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Experience varies among union members, so their predictions differ; revisit Section 14.2.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Predictions are b₁ + b₂ × experience + a for members, which changes with each member's experience.

practice.explanation: Sections 14.1–14.2: with only an indicator, predictions take two values; once a continuous regressor is added, predictions also vary within each group.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of exam scores on a tutoring indicator (1 = attended tutoring) gives a coefficient of 6 points. This shows that attending tutoring raises a student's score by 6 points.

options.text: True
options.feedback: The coefficient is a difference in group means. Students who chose tutoring may differ in motivation or prior grades; revisit Section 14.1.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The 6 points describe how the two groups' averages differ, not what tutoring does to a given student.

practice.explanation: Section 14.1: regression on an indicator is a descriptive comparison of group means. Differences between the groups in other factors can drive the gap.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of exam scores on a tutoring indicator gives t = 2.30 with default standard errors and t = 2.05 with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. Which pair best describes the t-statistics from the classical two-sample t-test and from Welch's t-test on the same data?

options.text: Classical: 2.05; Welch: about 2.30
options.feedback: The pairing is reversed. The classical test assumes equal variances, like default standard errors; Welch's test allows unequal variances, like robust ones.

options.text: Both: 2.30
options.feedback: Only the classical test matches the default-SE regression. Welch's test allows the two groups to have different variances.

options.text: Both: about 2.05
options.feedback: Only Welch's test is close to the robust-SE regression. The classical test assumes equal variances.

options.text: Classical: 2.30; Welch: about 2.05
options.feedback: Correct. The classical t-test equals the default-SE regression t; Welch's test is similar to the robust-SE regression t.

practice.explanation: Section 14.1: the classical t-test is identical to regression with default standard errors; Welch's t-test (unequal variances) is similar to regression with robust standard errors.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of exam scores on a tutoring indicator gives a coefficient of 6.0, and the same data are analyzed with Welch's two-sample t-test. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Welch's test also estimates the difference between the two group means as 6.0.
options.feedback: Correct. Both approaches give the same point estimate, the difference in means.

options.text: Welch's test makes it just as easy as the regression to control for prior grades.
options.feedback: A two-sample test compares two means only. Adding controls is what the regression framework makes easy.

options.text: The standard error from Welch's test can differ slightly from the regression's.
options.feedback: Correct. The two methods compute the standard error differently, so it can differ slightly.

options.text: If prior grades also differ between the two groups, part of the 6.0 gap may reflect them.
options.feedback: Correct. Both methods compare raw group means, which can reflect any other way the groups differ.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.2: specialized difference-in-means tests and regression on an indicator give the same estimate but slightly different standard errors. Both compare raw means; regression is more flexible because controls such as prior grades can be added.

practice.concept: Standard error of a difference in means (Key Concept 14.2)
practice.stem: Suppose group 1 has 36 students with a standard deviation of 12 points and group 0 has 25 students with a standard deviation of 10 points. What is Welch's standard error of the difference in means?

options.feedback: This adds the two groups' standard errors, 12/6 + 10/5. The formula adds their squares (the variances of the means) and then takes the square root.
This is √(12² + 10²), which leaves out the group sizes. Each variance is divided by its group's size.
8 is the sum of the variances of the two means; the standard error is its square root.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of hourly wages on a union indicator, using 5,000 workers, gives R² = 0.03 and a union coefficient with p < 0.001. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Union membership must be unrelated to wages in the population, because R² is close to zero.
options.feedback: A small R² means union status explains little of the spread in wages, not that it is unrelated to them; the p-value says the gap is clearly nonzero.

options.text: Union status explains little of the variation in individual wages, yet the gap in mean wages is precisely estimated.
options.feedback: Correct. Wages vary a lot within each group, so R² is small, but 5,000 workers pin down the difference in means.

options.text: Union members earn about 3% more per hour than nonmembers.
options.feedback: R² is a share of explained variation, not the size of the gap.

options.text: The small R² shows that union members' wages vary less than nonmembers' wages.
options.feedback: R² compares explained with total variation in wages; it says nothing about which group's wages are more spread out.

practice.explanation: R² and statistical significance answer different questions: how much variation is explained versus how precisely a coefficient is estimated. A small R² can coexist with a highly significant group difference.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression gives predicted hourly wage = 2.0 + 1.5 × education + 3.0 × union, where union = 1 for union members. Which statement interprets 3.0 correctly?

options.text: Union members earn $3.00 more per hour than nonmembers on average, ignoring education.
options.feedback: That describes the raw (unconditional) gap. With education in the model, the comparison holds education fixed.

options.text: Each year of education raises union members' wages by $3.00 more than nonmembers'.
options.feedback: The model has no union × education term, so the education slope is the same 1.5 for both groups.

options.text: Among workers with the same education, union members earn $3.00 more per hour on average.
options.feedback: Correct. The indicator's coefficient is the gap conditional on the other regressors.

options.text: Joining a union causes every worker's wage to rise by $3.00 per hour.
options.feedback: The regression describes an association in the data; it is not by itself a causal effect for every worker.

practice.explanation: Section 14.2: with additional regressors, the coefficient on d measures the difference in y across the categories after controlling for the other variables.

practice.stem: Suppose the raw union wage gap is $4.00 per hour but falls to $3.00 once experience is added as a control. Which explanation fits this change?

options.text: Adding any control always shrinks an indicator's coefficient.
options.feedback: Controls can move a coefficient in either direction, depending on how the control differs between groups and relates to y.

options.text: The regression with experience must use fewer workers than the raw comparison.
options.feedback: Nothing in the scenario says the sample changed; the change comes from comparing workers with equal experience.

options.text: Experience is unrelated to wages, so adding it changes nothing of substance.
options.feedback: If experience were unrelated to wages, adding it would leave the gap essentially unchanged.

options.text: Union members have more experience on average, and experience is associated with higher wages.
options.feedback: Correct. Part of the raw gap reflected the union members' extra experience; holding experience fixed removes that part.

practice.explanation: Section 14.2: a control changes an indicator's coefficient when it differs between the groups and is related to y. Here it explains part of the raw gap; in other data it can widen a gap.

practice.stem: Adding a control variable to a regression can enlarge the magnitude of an indicator's coefficient.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. A control can move the coefficient in either direction, depending on how it differs between the groups and relates to y.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the conditional versus unconditional gap in the Key Concepts and Section 14.2.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts (conditional vs. unconditional gap): controls strip out compositional differences, and that can make a gap smaller or larger.

practice.stem: Practice Exercise 5 reports predicted earnings = 10,000 + 5,000 × education − 8,000 × gender − 2,000 × (gender × education), with gender = 1 for women. What does −8,000 measure?

options.text: The average female–male earnings gap across all workers in the sample, whatever their education
options.feedback: With the interaction in the model, the gap changes with education; −8,000 is the gap at one particular education level.

options.text: How much less women gain from each extra year of education
options.feedback: That is the role of the interaction coefficient, −2,000.

options.text: The predicted earnings of a woman with no education
options.feedback: A woman with no education is predicted to earn 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000; −8,000 is a difference between women and men.

options.text: How much lower women's predicted earnings are than men's when education equals zero
options.feedback: Correct. Setting education = 0 removes both slope terms, leaving a gap of −8,000.

practice.explanation: Section 14.3: in y = β₁ + β₂x + α₁d + α₂(d × x), α₁ is the difference in intercepts, the gap at x = 0.

practice.stem: In the same fitted model, predicted earnings = 10,000 + 5,000 × education − 8,000 × gender − 2,000 × (gender × education), what is the return to one more year of education for women?

options.feedback: Correct: for women the education slope is 5,000 − 2,000 = 3,000.
This adds 2,000 instead of applying the interaction's negative sign.
5,000 is the return for men (gender = 0). For women the interaction term also changes with education.
−2,000 is the difference between the women's and men's slopes, not the women's slope itself.

practice.explanation: Section 14.3: for d = 1 the slope on x is b₂ + a₂ = 5,000 + (−2,000) = 3,000; for d = 0 it is b₂ = 5,000.

practice.stem: In the same fitted model, predicted earnings = 10,000 + 5,000 × education − 8,000 × gender − 2,000 × (gender × education), what is the predicted female–male earnings gap for workers with 12 years of education?

options.feedback: This keeps only the interaction part, −2,000 × 12; the gap at x also includes −8,000.
This uses one year of education. The interaction term must be multiplied by 12.
This adds the main effect to +24,000, flipping the sign of the interaction term.

practice.explanation: Section 14.3: the female–male gap at education x is a₁ + a₂x = −8,000 − 2,000x, which is −32,000 at x = 12.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression includes a gender indicator and a gender × education interaction, with t-statistics of −1.5 and −1.8, neither significant at 5% (Practice Exercise 6). What is the right next step?

options.text: Conclude that gender does not matter for earnings, since neither term is significant.
options.feedback: Two insignificant t-tests do not show that the two terms are jointly zero.

options.text: Conclude that gender matters, since both t-statistics are negative.
options.feedback: The signs of insignificant estimates are not evidence by themselves.

options.text: Test the two gender terms jointly with an F-test before drawing a conclusion.
options.feedback: Correct. Gender enters through two terms, so H₀: α₁ = 0 and α₂ = 0 should be tested together.

options.text: Re-estimate with default standard errors, which are always smaller.
options.feedback: Default standard errors are not always smaller, and switching standard errors to get significance is not a valid test.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.4: when a categorical variable enters through an indicator and its interaction, test their joint significance with an F-test rather than with individual t-tests.

practice.stem: Suppose a wage regression includes a south indicator and its interactions with education and with experience. The three south terms have p-values of 0.21, 0.08, and 0.12, and the joint test that all three are zero has p = 0.004. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each south term is individually significant at the 5% level.
options.feedback: All three individual p-values are above 0.05.

options.text: The three south terms are jointly significant at the 1% level.
options.feedback: Correct: the joint p-value, 0.004, is below 0.01.

options.text: The joint test shows that all three south coefficients are nonzero.
options.feedback: Rejecting a joint null says that at least one coefficient is nonzero, not that all of them are.

options.text: At the 5% level, the evidence says region matters for wages in this model.
options.feedback: Correct. The joint test, which asks whether region matters at all, rejects.

options.text: The joint test should use the smallest of the three individual p-values, 0.08.
options.feedback: A joint test has its own F-statistic and p-value (here 0.004); it is not read off the individual p-values.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.4: when a variable enters through several terms, the joint F-test answers whether it matters at all. Terms can be individually insignificant yet jointly significant.

practice.concept: Testing for structural change (Section 14.4, Key Concept 14.5)
practice.stem: Suppose a researcher estimates the same wage equation separately for union and nonunion workers and then runs a Chow test. What does its null hypothesis state?

options.text: Union and nonunion workers have the same mean wage.
options.feedback: That is the null of a simple difference-in-means test.

options.text: One common set of coefficients, intercept included, fits both groups.
options.feedback: Correct. Under H₀ the data can be pooled; under Hₐ the groups need separate coefficients.

options.text: Every slope coefficient in the wage equation is zero in both of the groups.
options.feedback: That is a test of overall significance, not a comparison between the groups.

options.text: The errors have the same variance in both groups.
options.feedback: Equal error variances are a separate question; the Chow test compares coefficients.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.5: the Chow test asks whether pooling (imposing the same coefficients on both groups) is justified. Rejecting it means the relationship differs across groups.

practice.stem: Suppose separate wage regressions for urban and rural workers give education slopes of 1.20 and 0.80 dollars per hour. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because the urban slope is larger, urban workers must have more education on average.
options.feedback: A slope describes how wages change with education within a group; it says nothing about the group's average education.

options.text: One regression with an urban indicator interacted with every regressor would give the same two sets of coefficients.
options.feedback: Correct. Fully interacting the indicator lets every coefficient differ by group, as the separate regressions do.

options.text: A Chow test can assess whether the two groups' coefficients differ by more than chance.
options.feedback: Correct. That is exactly its purpose.

options.text: Separate regressions can be run only when the two groups have the same number of workers.
options.feedback: Each regression simply uses its own group's observations; group sizes can differ.

practice.explanation: Section 14.4: separate regressions let all coefficients differ by group, which is equivalent to fully interacting a group indicator. The Chow test formally compares the groups' coefficients.

practice.concept: The dummy variable trap (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.6)
practice.stem: Suppose quarterly sales are regressed on an intercept, advertising, and indicators Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4 for the four quarters. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For every observation, Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 equals one.
options.feedback: Correct. Each observation falls in exactly one quarter.

options.text: Adding more observations would let OLS estimate all five of these terms.
options.feedback: The four indicators sum to one in every observation, so more data cannot break the exact collinearity.

options.text: Dropping the intercept and keeping all four quarter indicators is a valid fix.
options.feedback: Correct. Without an intercept, the four indicators no longer duplicate the constant.

options.text: The problem is that the quarter indicators are highly but not perfectly correlated.
options.feedback: The relationship is exact: the four indicators always sum to one, which equals the intercept's regressor.

options.text: Dropping Q4 makes the fourth quarter the reference for the other quarters' coefficients.
options.feedback: Correct. The omitted category becomes the base.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.6: indicators for all C categories plus an intercept are perfectly collinear because they sum to one. Drop one indicator (the base) or drop the intercept.

practice.concept: Sets of indicator variables (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.6)
practice.stem: Suppose respondents live in one of five regions. How many region indicators can a regression with an intercept include?

options.feedback: All five plus an intercept fall into the dummy variable trap.
Only one category needs to be omitted to avoid the trap, so more than three indicators can enter.
Only one category needs to be omitted, so more than two indicators can enter.
Correct: C − 1 = 4 indicators, with the omitted region as the base.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.6: with an intercept, include C − 1 of the C indicators; the omitted category is the base.

practice.stem: With three mutually exclusive indicators d₁, d₂, and d₃, OLS gives ŷ = 1 + 3d₂ + 5d₃ (Practice Exercise 3). What does the coefficient 3 measure?

options.text: How much the mean of y in category 2 exceeds the mean in category 1
options.feedback: Correct. Category 1 is omitted, so it is the base: its mean is 1 and category 2's mean is 1 + 3 = 4.

options.text: The mean of y in category 2
options.feedback: Category 2's mean is the intercept plus the coefficient, 1 + 3 = 4.

options.text: How much the mean of y in category 2 exceeds the overall mean
options.feedback: Coefficients compare each category with the omitted base category, not with the overall mean.

options.text: How much the mean of y in category 3 exceeds the mean in category 2
options.feedback: That difference is 5 − 3 = 2.

practice.explanation: Section 14.5: with d₁ omitted, the intercept is category 1's mean and each coefficient is a difference from category 1. The means are 1, 4, and 6.

practice.stem: For the same data, ŷ = 1 + 3d₂ + 5d₃, suppose we instead regress y on an intercept, d₁, and d₂, so d₃ is omitted (Practice Exercise 4). What is the coefficient on d₂?

options.feedback: 3 compared category 2 with category 1. With d₃ omitted, the comparison is with category 3.
Correct: category 2's mean (4) minus category 3's mean (6) is −2.
This adds the two old coefficients. Find each category's mean first, then subtract the new base's mean.
−5 is the new coefficient on d₁ (1 − 6). The question asks about d₂.

practice.explanation: Section 14.5: the means are 1, 4, and 6. With category 3 as base, ŷ = 6 − 5d₁ − 2d₂: the fit is unchanged, only the comparisons change.

practice.concept: Sets of indicator variables (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.7)
practice.stem: Suppose y is regressed on all three of d₁, d₂, and d₃ with no intercept and no other regressors. Then each coefficient equals the mean of y in that category.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. With only the full set of indicators, each coefficient is its own group's mean.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the no-intercept approach in Section 14.5 and Key Concept 14.7.

practice.explanation: Section 14.5 and Key Concept 14.7: regressing y on the full set of indicators alone, with no intercept, gives the group means directly (here 1, 4, and 6).

practice.stem: Suppose a national survey covers five regions, and 60% of the respondents live in region A. Which reason best supports using region A as the base category?

options.text: Using the largest region as the base makes the intercept equal to the overall sample mean.
options.feedback: The intercept is the base region's mean (or its intercept, with controls), not the overall mean.

options.text: Using region A as the base will raise the regression's R².
options.feedback: The choice of base does not change the fit, only the interpretation of the coefficients.

options.text: Each coefficient then compares a smaller region with the typical respondent's region.
options.feedback: Correct. A large, common base gives natural comparisons, which is the chapter's practical advice.

options.text: Region A's indicator will then have the smallest standard error.
options.feedback: The base region has no indicator, and therefore no coefficient or standard error, in the regression.

practice.explanation: Section 14.5 (practical advice): choose the largest or most common category, or the policy-relevant one, as the base, and always state which category is omitted.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression with categories A, B, and C uses A as the base. If the base is switched to C, the t-statistic on the B indicator generally changes, because it now compares B with C.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. An individual t-test on an indicator compares that category with whatever category is the base.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit what an individual coefficient on an indicator measures (Section 14.5).

practice.explanation: Section 14.5: changing the base changes the interpretation of the individual coefficients and their t-tests, because each is a difference from the base.

practice.concept: Regression on a set of indicators (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.7)
practice.stem: Suppose mean test scores are 70 in public schools, 74 in charter schools, and 79 in private schools. Scores are regressed on an intercept, a charter indicator, and a private indicator, with no other regressors. What is the coefficient on the private indicator?

options.feedback: 79 is the private schools' mean. With an intercept, the coefficient is a difference from the base.
5 compares private with charter schools, but the omitted base is public schools.
The difference is private minus public, 79 − 70, not public minus private.
Correct: 79 − 70 = 9, the gap between private schools and the public-school base.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.7: with no other regressors, the intercept is the base group's mean (70) and each coefficient is a difference in means: charter 4, private 9.

practice.concept: ANOVA as regression on indicators (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.7)
practice.stem: Suppose a one-way ANOVA of house prices across four regions gives F = 1.25 with p = 0.29. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the 5% level, we reject the hypothesis that the four regional means are equal.
options.feedback: p = 0.29 is above 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected.

options.text: The same F-statistic comes from a default-SE regression of price on three regional indicators and an intercept, testing that all three coefficients are zero.
options.feedback: Correct. ANOVA is the regression F-test on a set of indicators.

options.text: At the 5% level, the data give no evidence that mean prices differ across the regions.
options.feedback: Correct: p = 0.29 > 0.05.

options.text: The test proves that the four regional means are equal.
options.feedback: Failing to reject is a lack of evidence, not proof of equality.

options.text: The ANOVA null hypothesis is that all four population means are equal.
options.feedback: Correct: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.7: one-way ANOVA tests H₀ that all group means are equal; it is the same F-test as regressing y on C − 1 indicators plus an intercept.

practice.stem: Suppose a scatter plot of wages against experience, with a separate fitted line for union and nonunion workers, shows two parallel lines a constant distance apart. Which is the simplest specification that captures this pattern?

options.text: Experience and a union indicator, with no interaction
options.feedback: Correct. Parallel lines mean a common slope with an intercept shift, which an indicator alone provides.

options.text: Experience, a union indicator, and union × experience
options.feedback: The interaction allows different slopes, which parallel lines do not call for.

options.text: Experience alone, ignoring union status
options.feedback: This forces one line on both groups and cannot reproduce the constant gap between them.

options.text: Separate regressions for union and nonunion workers
options.feedback: Separate regressions let every coefficient differ; parallel lines need only an intercept shift.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 14.8: parallel lines indicate only an intercept shift (an indicator without interaction); non-parallel lines indicate differential slopes.

practice.stem: Suppose a box plot of exam scores marks each group's mean, and in every group the mean lies well below the median. This suggests that scores are skewed to the right within the groups.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit which tail pulls the mean away from the median (Section 14.5, box plots).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. A mean below the median points to a long left tail: a few very low scores pull the mean down.

practice.explanation: Section 14.5: a mean below the median points to a long left tail, as a few very low scores pull the mean down (left skew).

exam.stem: Which of these variables in the chapter's earnings data (AED_EARNINGS_COMPLETE, 872 workers) is not an indicator variable?

options.text: dgovt, for government employees
options.feedback: Revisit the values an indicator variable can take (Section 14.1).

options.text: genderbyeduc, the gender × education product
options.feedback: Correct. It equals years of education for women and 0 for men, so it takes many values.

options.text: gender, with 1 for women and 0 for men
options.feedback: Revisit the values an indicator variable can take (Section 14.1).

options.text: dself, for self-employed workers
options.feedback: Revisit the values an indicator variable can take (Section 14.1).

exam.explanation: Section 14.1: gender, dself, and dgovt take only the values 0 and 1. The interaction genderbyeduc = gender × education equals education for women and 0 for men.

exam.concept: Regression on a single indicator (Section 14.1, Key Concept 14.1)
exam.stem: Regressing earnings on gender (1 = female, 0 = male) gives predicted earnings = 63,476 − 16,396 × gender. What does 63,476 measure?

options.text: Average earnings of all 872 workers
options.feedback: Revisit what the intercept equals in a regression on a single indicator (Key Concept 14.1).

options.text: Average earnings of the men in the sample
options.feedback: Correct. The intercept is the mean of y for the group with gender = 0.

options.text: Average earnings of the women in the sample
options.feedback: Revisit what the intercept equals in a regression on a single indicator (Key Concept 14.1).

options.text: The earnings gap between men and women
options.feedback: Revisit what the intercept equals in a regression on a single indicator (Key Concept 14.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.1: in ŷ = b + ad, b is the mean of y when d = 0. With gender = 0 for men, $63,476 is the men's mean earnings.

exam.concept: Regression on a single indicator (Section 14.1, Key Concept 14.1)
exam.stem: Regressing earnings on gender (1 = female, 0 = male) gives predicted earnings = 63,476 − 16,396 × gender. Suppose we define male = 1 − gender and regress earnings on an intercept and male instead. Which fitted equation results?

options.feedback: Revisit what the intercept and the slope equal in a regression on a single indicator (Key Concept 14.1).
Revisit what the intercept and the slope equal in a regression on a single indicator (Key Concept 14.1).
Revisit what the intercept and the slope equal in a regression on a single indicator (Key Concept 14.1).
Correct. Women (male = 0) are now the base: their mean is 63,476 − 16,396 = 47,080, and men earn 16,396 more.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.1: the intercept is the mean of the group coded 0 and the slope is the difference in means. With women as the base, ŷ = 47,080 + 16,396 × male; the fitted values are unchanged.

exam.stem: In the chapter's regression of earnings on gender alone, the 872 fitted values take only two distinct values.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Every woman gets b + a and every man gets b: the two group means.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the predicted values of ŷ = b + a·d in Section 14.1.

exam.explanation: Section 14.1: with only an intercept and one indicator, ŷ takes the value b for d = 0 and b + a for d = 1.

exam.stem: Because the regression of earnings on gender compares women and men directly, its coefficient of −16,396 measures the causal effect of being female on a worker's earnings.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what the chapter says about descriptive versus causal readings of this gap (Section 14.1).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. It is a descriptive difference in means; it may reflect education, hours, occupation, discrimination, or other factors.

exam.explanation: Section 14.1: the coefficient is the unconditional (raw) gap in mean earnings. It is a descriptive finding, not necessarily causal.

exam.stem: Regressing earnings on gender gives t = −4.71 for the gender coefficient with default standard errors. Which statement about the classical two-sample t-test and Welch's t-test on the same data is correct?

options.text: The classical test gives exactly −4.71; Welch's test gives a somewhat different value, close to the robust-SE regression t.
options.feedback: Correct. The classical t-test is identical to the default-SE regression; Welch's test (unequal variances) is similar to the robust-SE regression.

options.text: Welch's test gives exactly −4.71; the classical test gives a somewhat different value, close to the robust-SE regression t.
options.feedback: Revisit which regression standard errors each two-sample t-test corresponds to (Section 14.1, Comparison with t-test).

options.text: Both tests give exactly −4.71, because each is equivalent to the default-SE regression.
options.feedback: Revisit which regression standard errors each two-sample t-test corresponds to (Section 14.1, Comparison with t-test).

options.text: Neither test gives −4.71, because two-sample t-tests and regressions use unrelated formulas.
options.feedback: Revisit which regression standard errors each two-sample t-test corresponds to (Section 14.1, Comparison with t-test).

exam.explanation: Section 14.1: classical t-test = regression with default standard errors (t = −4.71); Welch's t-test (unequal variances) ≈ regression with robust standard errors (both t ≈ −5.10).

exam.stem: The chapter compares the regression of earnings on gender with Welch's two-sample t-test. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Welch's t-test is valid only when women's and men's earnings have equal variances.
options.feedback: Revisit what Welch's test assumes about the two groups' variances (Section 14.1).

options.text: Both approaches estimate the gap as women's mean earnings minus men's mean earnings.
options.feedback: Correct. Both give the same point estimate, the difference in means.

options.text: The regression framework can add education or hours as controls, which a two-sample t-test cannot do.
options.feedback: Correct. That flexibility is the main advantage of regression.

options.text: The regression's standard error matches Welch's exactly, whether default or robust standard errors are used.
options.feedback: Revisit how Key Concept 14.2 compares regression on an indicator with a two-sample test.

options.text: Both approaches test the same null hypothesis: equal population mean earnings for women and men.
options.feedback: Correct. Each tests whether the difference in means is zero.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.2: specialized difference-in-means tests and regression on an indicator give the same point estimate and test the same hypothesis; regression is more flexible because controls can be added.

exam.concept: Standard error of a difference in means (Key Concept 14.2)

options.text: About $4,402

options.text: About $69,332
options.feedback: Revisit how Key Concept 14.2 combines the two groups' variances and sizes.

options.text: About $3,217
About $2,348
options.feedback: Revisit how Key Concept 14.2 combines the two groups' variances and sizes.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.2: se(ȳ₁ − ȳ₀) = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₀²/n₀) = √(31,597²/378 + 61,713²/494) ≈ $3,217, almost exactly the robust regression standard error.

exam.stem: In Model 1 (earnings on gender alone), R² = 0.025, yet the gender coefficient is significant with p < 0.001. Which statement best reconciles the two?

options.text: An R² this low means the model is misspecified, so the p-value of the gender coefficient cannot be trusted.
options.feedback: Revisit what R² measures and what a p-value measures (Section 14.1 and the model comparison in Section 14.3).

options.text: The R² measures the size of the gap: women earn about 2.5% less than men.
options.feedback: Revisit what R² measures and what a p-value measures (Section 14.1 and the model comparison in Section 14.3).

options.text: Gender explains little of the variation in individual earnings, but with 872 workers the gap in means is estimated precisely.
options.feedback: Correct. Earnings vary widely within each gender, so R² is small, yet the difference in means is precisely estimated.

options.text: The p-value tests the intercept, while the R² describes the gender coefficient alone.
options.feedback: Revisit what R² measures and what a p-value measures (Section 14.1 and the model comparison in Section 14.3).

exam.explanation: R² (0.025) is the share of earnings variation explained by gender; the p-value says the $16,396 gap is far from zero relative to its standard error. A small R² and a highly significant coefficient can coexist.

exam.stem: Model 2 gives predicted earnings = −17,552 − 18,258 × gender + 5,907 × education. Which statement interprets −18,258 correctly?

options.text: Comparing women and men with the same years of education, women earn about $18,258 less on average.
options.feedback: Correct. With education in the model, the indicator's coefficient is the gap conditional on education.

options.text: Women earn about $18,258 less than men on average, before education is taken into account.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 14.2 interprets the coefficient a in a model with additional regressors.

options.text: Each extra year of education is associated with $18,258 less in earnings for women than for men.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 14.2 interprets the coefficient a in a model with additional regressors.

options.text: Being female causes every worker's earnings to fall by $18,258 at any given level of education.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of descriptive and causal readings (Sections 14.1–14.2).

exam.explanation: Section 14.2: the coefficient a on d measures the difference in y across the categories after controlling for the other regressors, here education.

exam.stem: The gender coefficient is −16,396 in Model 1 and −18,258 in Model 2, which adds education. Which explanation fits the chapter's data?

options.text: Adding a control widens an indicator's coefficient whenever the control is related to earnings, whatever its link to gender.
options.feedback: Revisit the conditional versus unconditional gap (Key Concepts and Section 14.2).

options.text: Men in the sample average more years of education than women, and education is associated with higher earnings.
options.feedback: Revisit the conditional versus unconditional gap (Key Concepts and Section 14.2).

options.text: Model 2 drops the workers with missing education, so it is estimated on a different sample.
options.feedback: Revisit the conditional versus unconditional gap (Key Concepts and Section 14.2).

options.text: Women in the sample average more years of education than men, and education is associated with higher earnings.
options.feedback: Correct. Women's extra schooling predicts higher earnings, so holding education fixed widens the unexplained gap.

exam.explanation: Section 14.2: women average 14.0 years of education and men 13.7, and education has a positive coefficient, so comparing equally educated workers widens the gap from −16,396 to −18,258 (a suppression effect).

exam.stem: Adding the gender indicator to a regression of earnings on education, without any gender × education term, lets the education slope differ between women and men.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what an indicator alone does to the fitted lines, compared with an interaction (Key Concept 14.3).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. An indicator alone shifts the intercept but keeps the two lines parallel; different slopes need the interaction.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.3: including only d shifts the intercept but keeps the slopes parallel; adding d × x lets both the intercept and the slope differ.

exam.stem: Model 3 gives predicted earnings = −31,451 + 20,219 × gender + 6,921 × education − 2,765 × (gender × education), with gender = 1 for women. What does 20,219 measure?

options.text: The amount by which women out-earn men on average, holding education fixed
options.feedback: Revisit what the main gender coefficient means once an interaction is included (Section 14.3).

options.text: The predicted female–male earnings gap for workers with zero years of education
options.feedback: Correct. With education = 0 both education terms vanish, leaving a gap of 20,219, a value far outside where most workers are.

options.text: The predicted earnings of a woman with zero years of education
options.feedback: Revisit what the main gender coefficient means once an interaction is included (Section 14.3).

options.text: The predicted female–male gap at the sample's average education of about 14 years
options.feedback: Revisit what the main gender coefficient means once an interaction is included (Section 14.3).

exam.explanation: Section 14.3: a₁ is the difference in intercepts, the gap at education = 0. The chapter calls it "not very meaningful", since almost every worker has far more schooling.

exam.stem: Model 3 gives predicted earnings = −31,451 + 20,219 × gender + 6,921 × education − 2,765 × (gender × education), with gender = 1 for women. By how much do predicted earnings rise with one more year of education for women?

options.feedback: Correct: 6,921 − 2,765 = 4,156 per year for women, versus 6,921 for men.
Revisit how the fitted equation splits into separate lines for women and men (Section 14.3).
Revisit how the fitted equation splits into separate lines for women and men (Section 14.3).
Revisit how the fitted equation splits into separate lines for women and men (Section 14.3).

exam.explanation: Section 14.3: for d = 1 the slope is b₂ + a₂ = 6,921 + (−2,765) = 4,156. The interaction coefficient is the difference between the women's and men's slopes.

exam.stem: Model 3 gives predicted earnings = −31,451 + 20,219 × gender + 6,921 × education − 2,765 × (gender × education), with gender = 1 for women. What is the predicted female–male earnings gap for workers with 16 years of education?

options.feedback: Revisit how the gap between the two fitted lines depends on education (Section 14.3).
Revisit how the gap between the two fitted lines depends on education (Section 14.3).
Revisit how the gap between the two fitted lines depends on education (Section 14.3).

exam.explanation: Section 14.3: the female–male gap at education x is a₁ + a₂x = 20,219 − 2,765x. At 16 years it is −24,021: positive only at very low education, increasingly negative above about 7 years.

exam.stem: In Model 3 (earnings on gender, education, and gender × education), the gender coefficient has t = 1.32 (p = 0.19). Why does this not show that gender is unrelated to earnings once education is controlled for?

options.text: The gender coefficient is estimated from the 378 women only, so its standard error is large.
options.feedback: Revisit how the joint-testing discussion explains misleading individual t-tests (Key Concept 14.4).

options.text: Robust standard errors are too conservative for indicator variables, so this t-statistic understates significance.
options.feedback: Revisit how the joint-testing discussion explains misleading individual t-tests (Key Concept 14.4).

options.text: Gender also enters through gender × education, which is highly correlated with gender, so neither term is precise alone.
options.feedback: Correct. The two gender terms are nearly collinear, so each is imprecisely estimated on its own.

options.text: The t-test compares the gender coefficient with the education coefficient, not with zero.
options.feedback: Revisit how the joint-testing discussion explains misleading individual t-tests (Key Concept 14.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.4: when an indicator and its interaction are both included, individual t-tests can mislead because the two are highly correlated (r = 0.97 here). The joint test of both gender terms rejects decisively (p < 0.001).

exam.stem: In Model 5, the terms gender, gender × education, gender × age, and gender × hours have robust p-values of 0.074, 0.053, 0.86, and 0.094, while the joint test that all four coefficients are zero has p < 0.001. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the 5% level, none of the four gender terms is individually significant.
options.feedback: Correct. All four individual p-values exceed 0.05.

options.text: The joint test rejects, at the 1% level, the hypothesis that all four gender coefficients are zero.
options.feedback: Correct. The joint p-value is below 0.001.

options.text: Since no term is individually significant at 5%, the joint result must be a computational error.
options.feedback: Revisit why joint and individual tests can disagree (Key Concept 14.4).

options.text: Whether gender matters in Model 5 should be judged by the joint test rather than by the four separate t-tests.
options.feedback: Correct. Gender enters through four terms, so the joint test answers whether it matters at all.

options.text: The joint test shows that each of the four gender coefficients is nonzero.
options.feedback: Revisit what rejecting a joint null hypothesis does and does not establish (Key Concept 14.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.4: individually insignificant terms can be jointly highly significant. Rejecting H₀ that all four are zero says gender matters (through the intercept, slopes, or both), not that every term is nonzero.

exam.concept: Testing for structural change (Section 14.4, Key Concept 14.5)
exam.stem: Section 14.4 estimates earnings on education, age, and hours separately for women and for men. What null hypothesis does the Chow test for these regressions examine?

options.text: Women's and men's mean earnings are equal.
options.feedback: Revisit what the Chow test compares (Section 14.4, Key Concept 14.5).

options.text: Education, age, and hours have no effect on earnings in the pooled sample.
options.feedback: Revisit what the Chow test compares (Section 14.4, Key Concept 14.5).

options.text: The variance of the errors is the same for women and men.
options.feedback: Revisit what the Chow test compares (Section 14.4, Key Concept 14.5).

options.text: The intercept and the three slopes are the same for women and men.
options.feedback: Correct. H₀: β<sup>F</sup> = β<sup>M</sup>, so the data could be pooled into one regression.

exam.explanation: Section 14.4: the Chow test's H₀ is β<sup>F</sup> = β<sup>M</sup> (pooled model) against Hₐ: β<sup>F</sup> ≠ β<sup>M</sup> (separate models).

exam.stem: The separate regressions of earnings on education, age, and hours give an hours slope of 691 for women and 1,621 for men, and an age slope of 500 for women and 549 for men. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each regression is estimated from one gender's workers only.
options.feedback: Correct: 378 women in one regression and 494 men in the other.

options.text: Because the hours slopes differ in these samples, the population hours slopes for women and men differ.
options.feedback: Revisit the role of sampling variation in comparing estimates across groups (Section 14.4).

options.text: A pooled regression with no gender terms would impose the same hours slope on women and men.
options.feedback: Correct. Pooling without interactions forces one set of slopes on both groups.

options.text: These regressions show that being female causes a lower return to an extra weekly hour of work.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of descriptive and causal readings (Sections 14.1–14.2).

exam.explanation: Section 14.4: separate regressions let every coefficient differ by gender. Sample slopes always differ somewhat; the Chow test judges whether the differences exceed what chance would produce.

exam.concept: The dummy variable trap (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.6)
exam.stem: Each worker is self-employed (dself = 1), a private-sector employee (dprivate = 1), or a government employee (dgovt = 1). Which statements about the dummy variable trap are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For every one of the 872 workers, dself + dprivate + dgovt = 1.
options.feedback: Correct. The three categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

options.text: With an intercept, including all three indicators makes the regressors perfectly collinear.
options.feedback: Correct. The intercept's column of ones equals the sum of the three indicators.

options.text: The trap goes away if heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are used.
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of problem the dummy variable trap is (Key Concept 14.6).

options.text: Dropping the intercept and keeping all three indicators avoids the trap.
options.feedback: Correct. This is one of the chapter's three equivalent approaches.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.6: since d₁ + d₂ + d₃ = 1, an intercept plus all three indicators are perfectly collinear. Drop one indicator (the base) or drop the intercept.

exam.concept: Sets of indicator variables (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.6)
exam.stem: Suppose the private sector were split in two, so worker type had four categories: self-employed, private for-profit, private nonprofit, and government. At most how many worker-type indicators could a regression with an intercept include?

options.feedback: Revisit how many indicators can enter alongside an intercept (Key Concept 14.6).
Correct: C − 1 = 3, with the omitted category as the base.
Revisit how many indicators can enter alongside an intercept (Key Concept 14.6).

options.feedback: Revisit how many indicators can enter alongside an intercept (Key Concept 14.6).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.6: with an intercept, include C − 1 indicators from a set of C mutually exclusive categories; here 4 − 1 = 3.

options.text: Self-employed workers earn about $17,098 more than government employees of the same education and age.
options.feedback: Revisit what the coefficient on an included indicator measures (Section 14.5).

exam.explanation: Section 14.5: the coefficient of an included indicator measures the difference relative to the base category, here private-sector employees, holding education and age fixed.

exam.stem: With private-sector employees as the base, predicted earnings = −47,249 + 17,098 × dself − 2,025 × dgovt + 5,865 × education + 488 × age. If self-employed workers were made the base instead (regressing on dprivate, dgovt, education, and age), what would the coefficient on dgovt be?

exam.explanation: Section 14.5: with self-employed as the base, dgovt compares government with self-employed workers: −2,025 − 17,098 = −19,123, as the chapter's Approach 3 reports. The fit is unchanged.

exam.stem: In the no-intercept regression of earnings on dself, dprivate, dgovt, education, and age, the coefficient on dself, −30,151, is the average earnings of the self-employed workers.

exam.explanation: Section 14.5: dropping the intercept gives each group its own intercept. Only with no other regressors do these coefficients equal group means; here the self-employed mean is $72,306.

exam.stem: The chapter uses private-sector employees as the base category for worker type. Which reason best supports that choice?

options.text: Omitting the largest category is what avoids the dummy variable trap.

options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's practical advice on choosing a base category (Section 14.5).

options.text: Omitting private-sector employees gives a higher R² than omitting either of the other categories.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's practical advice on choosing a base category (Section 14.5).

options.text: Private-sector employees are the largest group in the sample, which makes them a natural reference.
options.feedback: Correct. The chapter advises choosing the largest or most common category (here 663 of 872 workers), or the policy-relevant one.

exam.explanation: Section 14.5 (practical advice): choose the largest or most common category as the base, or the policy-relevant comparison, and always state which category is omitted.

exam.concept: Testing a set of indicators (Section 14.5, Key Takeaways)
exam.stem: In the worker-type regression with education and age, the joint test that both included worker-type indicators are zero gives the same F-statistic whether private-sector or self-employed workers are the base category.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit what changes and what stays the same when the base category is switched (Section 14.5).

exam.explanation: Section 14.5 and Key Takeaways: the joint F-test of the C − 1 included indicators is invariant to the choice of base; only the individual coefficients and their t-tests change.

exam.concept: Regression on a set of indicators (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.7)
exam.stem: Mean earnings are $72,306 for self-employed workers, $54,521 for private-sector employees, and $56,105 for government employees. In a regression of earnings on an intercept, dself, and dgovt only, what is the coefficient on dgovt?

Correct: 56,105 − 54,521 = 1,584, the government mean minus the private-sector (base) mean.

Revisit what the coefficients equal when y is regressed on a set of indicators with an intercept (Key Concept 14.7).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.7: with no other regressors, the intercept is the base group's mean ($54,521) and each coefficient is a difference in means: dgovt = 1,584 and dself = 17,785.

exam.concept: ANOVA as regression on indicators (Section 14.5, Key Concept 14.7)
exam.stem: A one-way ANOVA of earnings across the three worker types gives F = 4.24 with p = 0.015. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the 5% level, we reject the hypothesis that mean earnings are equal across the three worker types.
options.feedback: Correct: p = 0.015 < 0.05.

options.text: At the 1% significance level as well, we reject the hypothesis that mean earnings are equal across the three worker types.
options.feedback: Revisit how a p-value is compared with a significance level (Section 14.5).

options.text: A default-SE regression of earnings on an intercept, dself, and dgovt, jointly testing both coefficients, gives the same F of 4.24.
options.feedback: Correct. ANOVA is the regression F-test on a set of indicators with no other controls.

options.text: The result shows that each worker type's mean earnings differ from every other type's.
options.feedback: Revisit the alternative hypothesis of the ANOVA test (Section 14.5).

options.text: The ANOVA null hypothesis is that at least one worker type's mean earnings differ.
options.feedback: Revisit how the ANOVA null and alternative hypotheses are stated (Section 14.5).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 14.7: ANOVA tests H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ against "at least one mean differs". Its F equals the joint F-test from regressing earnings on the indicators; p = 0.015 rejects at 5% but not at 1%.
